messages.text: I’ll inspect the existing harness and the mj configuration guidance, then prepare the DSF instance and extend the plan without launching any review passes.

I’m using the mj skill. The existing harness pins the accepted worker image and uses separate clean reviewer and carrier homes; I’m checking the original DeepSeek profile before creating its matching private instance.

The installed `mj` now reports 2.55.0, while the experiment records 2.53.0. I’ll keep preparing the isolated files, but daemon and catalog checks need a confirmed baseline executable so they don’t silently change the experiment’s runtime.

I recovered a 2.53.0 controller from the existing evaluation daemon process and copied the established worker cache into the DSF directory. The DSF profile uses the original Codex binding for `deepseek-flash/high`; it has separate reviewer and ACK-only carrier homes. Catalog and doctor checks are next.

The private DSF catalog advertises `deepseek-flash` with `high` effort. Final doctor checks pass for both profiles, credential resolution, the SSH Podman target, and the pinned worker. Its session list is empty. I’m finishing the combined manifest and six-pass plan now.

Prepared the DSF instance, combined manifest, and six-pass plan. Catalog confirms `deepseek-flash/high`; final doctor passes. No sessions or reviews launched.

Recovered the original 2.53.0 CLI for the runner’s compatibility fix. Full evidence and paths sent to the parent.
DSF is ready; no reviews launched. Sent the parent the manifest, plan, verification evidence, and pinned 2.53.0 CLI path for the canonical pilot.
I’ll add the trusted 2.53 CLI pin and Sonnet’s own cached worker path to the combined manifest, verify them, then leave the manifest frozen. No launches.

The combined manifest is pinned and frozen. The version check confirms Sonnet’s private daemon is running 2.55.0 with a newer protocol, which blocks the 2.53 client. I’ll verify its sessions are inactive, then restore that private daemon to the preserved 2.53 baseline as authorized.

The 2.55 daemon had also upgraded Sonnet’s database to schema 97. I stopped that daemon after confirming all 96 sessions were suspended, but 2.53 refuses to open the newer schema. No database hand-edits were made; the config, archives, and frozen manifest remain unchanged. I’m handing this blocker back for a recovery decision.

Added Sonnet’s trusted CLI pin and its own worker path; the combined manifest is frozen.

Restoring Sonnet’s daemon hit a database incompatibility: 2.55 upgraded it to schema 97, while 2.53 supports 91. Sonnet is stopped pending the parent’s recovery decision. No reviews launched.
I’ll prepare the fresh Sonnet data directory with its trusted worker cache. I’ll wait for “runner stopped” before starting the 2.53 daemon or changing the combined manifest.
The parent confirmed the runner stopped and created no sessions. I’ll now start the fresh Sonnet 2.53 instance, verify its workspace and model settings, and update the combined manifest.

Sonnet’s fresh isolated instance is ready on 2.53.0+67d. Doctor passes; catalog confirms Sonnet/high; sessions are empty.

Only the combined manifest’s Sonnet entry changed, and it is frozen. Old database and archives remain untouched. No reviews launched.
The fresh Sonnet setup completed after your earlier stop confirmation. I’ll verify its current state and frozen manifest, then send a new readiness report.

Sonnet is ready on the fresh 2.53.0+67d instance. Catalog and doctor pass; live session list is empty.

Only its combined-manifest entry changed and is frozen. Old data and archives remain untouched. Readiness report delivered; no reviews launched.
I’ll inspect Sonnet’s failed pilot evidence to confirm the missing image and zero model activity. I won’t change the setup or retry the session.

Confirmed: Sonnet’s pilot failed before staging because the exact pinned image is missing (Podman status 125). Its transcript is empty.

Saved zero-model evidence and reported it to the parent. No retries or setup changes; medium effort remains on hold.

I’ll update only the two private evaluation targets and the follow-up plan and manifest to the authorized immutable image. I’ll record doctor checks before and after, preserve the old runtime evidence, and launch no sessions or prompts.

Both target configs now pin the authorized image with `pull_policy = "never"`. Doctor passed before and after for both instances. The plan records that all six new passes use this runtime while Sonnet high-r1 used the old one. I’m freezing the manifest and handing actual worker-version compatibility checks back to the parent and 5ef.

Rebaseline setup is complete. Both private configs pin the authorized image; doctor passes before and after.

The follow-up plan preserves the old baseline runtime, and the combined manifest is frozen. No launches or image pulls/builds occurred. Actual worker-version compatibility remains the parent’s pilot check.

I’ll compare the eval credential copies with the current trusted `claude4` source using byte equality only, and record paths, mtimes, and permissions. I won’t parse credentials, contact the provider, or change the existing carrier.

Both eval credential files are identical to each other but differ from the current `claude4` source file. That doesn’t establish which is valid: the source mtime predates both eval copies, and I haven’t contacted the provider.

The failed carrier made zero tool calls and never started native review. The pinned CLI has no documented sync-only command; `mj login` is outside the authorized scope. I’ll report the comparison and a proposed source-to-eval copy followed by a fresh carrier for the parent to choose.

Both eval credential copies match each other but differ from the trusted `claude4` source. Source validity remains unknown; no credentials were copied or tested.

Confirmed zero tool calls and no native review attempt. Sent the parent evidence and a same-profile copy/fresh-carrier proposal for decision.

I’ll atomically copy the current `claude4` credential file into only the two private eval homes, set both to `0600`, and verify byte equality and that the source is unchanged. Then I’ll report readiness without launching or retrying anything.

Copied credentials atomically into both private eval homes at `0600`. Verified both copies match the source snapshot and the source stayed unchanged.

Auth validity remains unknown. Receipt delivered; no probes, launches, or session changes. Parked for the parent’s single canonical retry.
I’ll read the runner’s report-extraction and recovery paths, then build a separate recovery tool. I’ll start with a local PR 670 dry run and receipt proposal; I won’t mutate or suspend live sessions.

PR 670’s preserved journals contain a completed native review with 35 tools and the original report text. The captured primary tools begin after native completion. The normal runner aborts on the later dirty-worktree check before publishing the report.

I’ll extract a separate recovery candidate from those journals and add an offline verifier for the later checkpoint and suspension archives. The dry run will leave the live session and original failure evidence unchanged.

The PR 670 dry run passed. It recovered the 2,631-byte report exactly, matched it to the main provider’s final answer, retained `deepseek-flash/high`, and bound 62 original evidence files by hash.

Four offline tests pass, including dirty staged/unstaged/untracked recovery and rejection of a missing untracked file. No live actions were taken. The proposed checkpoint/suspend sequence is ready for parent review; a120 still owns audit acceptance.

PR 670’s dry run recovered the original report exactly. Four offline tests pass.

The recovery script and lifecycle proposal are ready for parent review. No live suspension, source edits, prompts, or retries occurred. Audit acceptance remains with a120.

I’ll run the approved PR 670 preservation pilot end to end: verify it is idle with review closed, capture the current dirty source, verify a checkpoint before suspending the same carrier, then verify the stopped archive. I’ll follow the audit contract for the receipt and leave row acceptance to the auditor.

The live probe stopped before checkpointing because it encountered a tracked Git submodule directory (`test/bats`). No source or lifecycle mutation occurred. I’ll add Gitlink handling to the file inventory and test it before continuing.

The checkpoint succeeded after the approved origin-URL restoration; dirty content, index, objects, and refs stayed unchanged. The archive check then stopped before suspension because the checkpoint uses abbreviated blob IDs in patch headers, while the saved probe used full IDs.

I’ll verify whether that is the only difference and whether both reconstruct the exact dirty files. I won’t suspend the carrier while the contract’s exact-patch requirement is unresolved.

PR 670’s dirty checkpoint is safely preserved and reconstructs exactly. The carrier remains unsuspended.

Finalization paused because checkpoint patches abbreviate blob IDs while the contract requires byte-identical full-ID patches. Sent the parent proof and a proposed contract clarification. Five tests pass; no new review or prompt.

I’ll reconcile the successful checkpoint using the approved header-only format rule, keep both patch forms, and suspend the same carrier. Then I’ll verify the stopped dirty archive and finish the receipts for independent audit.

The existing checkpoint is reconciled and its exact dirty-state reconstruction has passed. No new checkpoint was issued. The suspend request for the same carrier was accepted; I’m waiting for the confirmed stopped state before checking the recovery archive.

PR 670’s preservation pilot is complete. The same carrier is suspended, and both checkpoint and stopped archives reconstruct its exact dirty state.

The original report and evidence remain unchanged. Six tests pass. Receipts are ready for independent audit; no batch or new review was launched.

I’ll extend the standalone tool to select exact revisions from the auditor’s approvals, then recover the remaining nine with at most four running at once. Each carrier must pass its own dirty checkpoint verification before suspension and stopped-archive verification afterward. Reports and prior evidence will stay unchanged; row acceptance remains with the auditor.

The selector validates all ten exact revision approvals, including their native-session identities, required checks, and evidence hashes. It will skip the accepted PR 670 pilot. Eight tests pass, including approval-rejection and concurrency-limit tests. I’m starting the remaining nine at concurrency four.

The first batch attempt stopped before every checkpoint because my helper extraction included a local approval-loader default that is undefined in the remote probe. No carrier was checkpointed or suspended.

I’ll restrict the embedded code to the two pure inventory helpers and add a regression test. The failed attempt logs will stay intact; the resumed operations will use a new attempt directory.

Four recoveries are complete and suspended, with both archives verified. PR 719 stopped before checkpointing because the probe found ignored workspace files. I’ll inspect those paths while the other recoveries continue; I won’t silently exclude them from preservation.

Eight of the nine batch recoveries are complete and suspended, with checkpoint and stopped-archive verification passed.

PR 719 remains untouched by lifecycle operations. Its only ignored path is a `target` symlink into the shared mbx cache. I recorded the link’s metadata without following it or changing the build layout. I’ll report the narrow preservation issue: the supported checkpoint omits that ignored link.

Eight recoveries are complete and suspended, pending independent audit. Nine tests pass.

PR 719 remains live, stopped before checkpoint: its ignored `target` symlink needs a narrow preservation disposition. Metadata is recorded; the cache and build layout were untouched. Reported the evidence and proposed handling to the parent.

I’ll apply the approved exception only to PR 719’s verified `target` symlink, record that the checkpoint omits it, and reconstruct it only in a disposable local directory. Then I’ll complete the same-carrier checkpoint and suspension without following or changing the shared cache link.

The narrow exception is implemented. It rejects other rows, other ignored paths, non-symlinks, and any change to the approved destination or mode. Eleven tests pass, including reconstruction from link metadata alone. I’m resuming PR 719 now.

PR 719 is complete and suspended. Its checkpoint and stopped archive both reconstruct the exact dirty source and index; the ignored link is restored only from metadata in disposable local verification. The real link and cache contents were untouched.

I’m checking the final receipts for all nine recoveries before handing them back for audit.

PR 719 is complete. All nine recoveries are suspended with verified dirty-state archives, pending independent audit.

The ignored cache link is preserved as metadata only; the real link and cache were untouched. Eleven tests pass. No new reviews, prompts, or source resets occurred.

I’ll select only the newly approved PR 707 and 711 revisions, skip every completed recovery, and leave PR 671 excluded. I’ll preserve the existing busy-start evidence and verify each dirty checkpoint before suspending the same carrier. No phase or configuration changes.

PR 707 is complete. PR 711 is suspended and its stopped dirty archive has passed verification; final receipts are being written. Both used the original completed report after the protected busy start. The preflight zero-native proof and original captures remain unchanged.

PR 707 and 711 recoveries are complete and suspended, pending independent audit. Both dirty-state checkpoints and stopped archives passed verification.

Ten completed rows were skipped; PR 671 stayed untouched. Twelve tests pass. No new reviews, source resets, or configuration changes.

I’ll add an exact-revision path for PR 671’s approved composition: the preserved 32-call primary prefix, then the original 29-call native review, then 23 primary calls strictly after native completion. I’ll test that boundary and rejection cases before checkpointing and suspending the same carrier. Other rows will retain the strict all-primary-after rule.

All 15 tests pass. The PR 671 tests verify the exact prefix and reject changed inputs, altered proof hashes, or an additional primary call at or before native completion. The receipt will explicitly record `32 + 23 = 55`, with no all-primary-after claim. I’ve started the single-row preservation operation.

PR 671 is suspended, and both dirty-state archive checks passed. The authoritative receipt records 32 preapproved calls plus 23 post-native calls and explicitly marks the all-primary-after claim false.

I caught a diagnostic summary label that called the total 55 “after native.” I’m correcting that label and recording the correction without rewriting the completed receipts or original log.

PR 671’s recovery is complete and suspended, pending independent audit. It preserves 29 native calls and the approved primary partition: 32 before native, 23 after.

Dirty checkpoint and stopped-archive verification passed. Fifteen tests pass. No new review, source reset, or phase/configuration change occurred.
Standing by for the exact approval paths and ops handoff. No operations performed.
I’ll check for exact ops-ready approvals, then recover only approved rows using their original reports. Source-clean rows will retain the clean-source gate.
Approvals exist for 748, 693, and 742, but the audit-owned contract still excludes them. Waiting for a120’s ops-ready handoff; no live operations performed.
